title: Halftone dithered weight storage spreads cell failures like printer dots
idea: Borrow halftone/error-diffusion printing: keep the sign and top bits of each AI weight in protected cells, but store the low-order magnitude as a thermometer (dot-density) code across 3 unprotected, refresh-relaxed cells, with error diffusion pushing each weight's rounding residual into its tile neighbours. A failed cell then moves a weight by one fine step that averages out across the tile, instead of flipping a binary bit.
why: Lets ~70% of weight-memory cells run at raw BER ~1e-3 with 4-8x longer refresh and no ECC parity (fact 3 refresh energy, ECC area); trades a little density on low-order bits for large refresh and ECC savings on inference memory.

title: Registration-mark pilot cells recalibrate sense references for every row
idea: Like the registration marks that align a press's colour plates, write 2-4 known pilot cells (one charged, one discharged) into each row at every restore; on activation a small comparator measures the pilot bitline swings and shifts that row's sense-amp reference and sensing delay on the fly, so rows whose cells have drifted (leakage, temperature, ageing) still sense correctly.
why: Turns marginal retention-tail reads into recoverable margin, allowing ~2-4x longer refresh or cells with ~30% less Cs (facts 1, 3) for ~0.5% cell overhead.

title: Movable-type sense amplifiers: swappable spare periphery slices
idea: Gutenberg's movable type made every letter replaceable; build the sense-amp, column-decoder and local wordline-driver strips as identical slices behind a small antifuse-configured crossbar, so a failed or slow periphery slice is swapped for a spare instead of scrapping the mat, which row/column redundancy cannot fix.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die (fact 7) and periphery defects are mostly unrepairable today; recovering them could add an estimated 3-8 yield points on 32-64 Gb and 3D dies, lowering cost per bit.

title: Ink-saver encoding keeps fewest cells in leaky charged state
idea: Like ink-saving fonts that print letters with holes, encode each burst with a low-weight code (e.g., 16b to 18b with per-group inversion) chosen using the die's true-cell/anti-cell map, so as few cells as possible sit in the charged state that leaks; retention failures are nearly all charged-to-discharged.
why: Cuts the population of retention-vulnerable cells by ~30-40%, so the same leakage tail (fact 3) yields fewer failures and refresh can stretch ~1.5x; restore energy drops slightly (fact 10) for ~6-12% capacity cost.

title: Triaxial-weave parity: row, column and diagonal threads catch clusters
idea: Triaxial fabrics weave threads at 0, 60 and 120 degrees so tears cannot run; overlay three interleaved parity families on each subarray mat (rows, columns, 60-degree diagonals), updated by on-die XOR trees at write-back, so a particle defect, a dead wordline segment or a hammered neighbourhood is located where three failing parity threads intersect and is corrected during scrub.
why: 2D clusters defeat on-die SEC; three-direction parity corrects them for ~3% overhead versus 6-12% for strong symbol codes, letting clustered-defect dies ship and absorbing hammer bursts (fact 9).

title: Plywood cross-grain tier rotation turns 3D line faults into single bits
idea: Plywood alternates grain 90 degrees so a split cannot run through the panel; in monolithic 3D DRAM, rotate each tier's wordline direction (or its logical bit-to-codeword map) relative to its neighbours and assemble codewords vertically across tiers, so one broken wordline in tier k becomes one bit in each of many codewords.
why: Tier-level line defects are the expected killer of 26+-tier 3D DRAM (fact 2); converting them into correctable single-bit errors could tolerate ~10x higher line-defect density per tier.

title: Ripstop quarantine bay: hot rows migrate into victimless sparse rows
idea: Ripstop fabric uses a reinforced grid where tears stop; reserve ~1% of each bank as a 'ripstop bay' in which only every third row holds data, and when the activation tracker flags an aggressor, migrate its data into the bay where it has no data-bearing physical neighbours to disturb.
why: Makes detected aggressors physically harmless instead of paying repeated victim refreshes (fact 9, ~1k ACT threshold); ~1-2% capacity versus up to 10-20% bandwidth for refresh-based mitigation.

title: Double-stitched hot rows halve activations per physical copy
idea: Tailors double-stitch seams at stress points; for read-hot rows the controller keeps a duplicate in a distant subarray and alternates or randomises activations between copies (writes go to both), so each physical row sees 1/k of the activation rate.
why: Raises the effective hammer threshold k-fold for read-mostly hot data such as weights and page tables without counters or neighbour refresh (fact 9); the twin also backs up a retention-failed copy.

title: Foundry riser canary rows fail first and trigger group refresh
idea: Castings use risers so shrinkage defects form in sacrificial metal; give every 64-row group one 'riser' canary row of deliberately undersized capacitors with an added leak device, sitting in the same local thermal environment. A background scanner activates only canary rows and refreshes a group only when its canary has decayed past a guard threshold.
why: Refresh tracks real local leakage and temperature instead of the 64 ms worst-case tail (fact 3); scanning is 1/64 of activations, targeting ~3-6x fewer refresh operations for ~1.5% row overhead.

title: Chemostat refresh holds corrected-error population at a setpoint
idea: A chemostat holds a culture at steady density by tuning its dilution rate; let each bank's refresh interval float under closed-loop control that targets a fixed rate of ECC-corrected errors seen by patrol scrubbing, lengthening refresh until corrections appear and shortening it when errors or temperature rise.
why: Most cells retain for seconds; tracking actual behaviour instead of the worst case could cut refresh energy and bandwidth (16-33% of idle power, fact 3) by 50-80%, with ECC as the safety net.

title: Solera placement: weak rows host hot data refreshed by use
idea: In a solera the youngest wine sits in the most-handled barrels; map frequently activated pages onto rows with the worst measured retention, since each activation restores their charge more often than refresh would, and put cold pages on the strongest rows, which then get 4-8x longer refresh intervals.
why: Uses retention-tail rows (fact 3) instead of sparing them and cuts refresh on the cold majority; ~2-4x refresh reduction with no added cells.

title: Zone-refining sweep anneals one bank at a time on-die
idea: Zone refining drags a molten band through an ingot; after migrating a bank's data out, drive millisecond Joule pulses through its buried wordlines (or dedicated under-array heater lines) to locally anneal the bank, de-trapping the oxide and junction defects behind variable retention time, then sweep the hot zone to the next bank.
why: Resets VRT and leakage-tail degradation over life, so refresh can be set by the healthy distribution (~2x longer) and weak dies stay in service longer (fact 3).

title: Adaptive-infill ECC: code strength varies page by page
idea: 3D printers vary infill density where stress is high; classify every 4 KB page at test and in the field by measured weakness and store it with a matching code rate (none, SEC-DED, or ~12% BCH), tracked in a page-attribute table, so strong pages hand their parity bits back as capacity.
why: Uniform worst-case ECC wastes ~12.5% of bits; adaptive rate recovers ~6-9% capacity on typical dies while still tolerating weak tails (cost per bit).

title: Selective-assembly die pairing matches complementary defect maps
idea: Bearing makers measure parts and mate oversized balls with undersized races; record each die's failing and weak-row map at wafer test and pair dies into stacks or ranks whose bad addresses do not overlap, so cheap module-level mirroring or spare sharing covers one die's holes with its partner's good rows.
why: Rescues dies that exceed on-die redundancy (several yield points) and makes cross-die repair nearly free because overlaps are engineered to near zero.

title: Miura-ori keyed fold scrambles physical row adjacency every boot
idea: A Miura-ori fold sends sheet neighbours far apart; add a tiny programmable mapping layer in each subarray's row decoder that applies a per-boot secret keyed permutation, so logically adjacent rows are physically distant and an attacker cannot tell which rows sandwich a victim; correlated physical faults are also spread across codewords.
why: Targeted double-sided hammering (fact 9) needs adjacency knowledge; a keyed fold makes it probabilistically infeasible without per-row counters.

title: Lattice-defect-aware codes for self-assembled cell arrays
idea: Block-copolymer self-assembly makes near-perfect hexagonal arrays whose defects are known topological types (dislocations, disclinations, grain boundaries) that displace lines or wedges of cells; design hexagonal-lattice codes whose syndromes recognise exactly those fault shapes, so DSA-patterned arrays with ~1e-4 defect density stay usable.
why: Lets self-assembly replace several EUV/ArF patterning passes (fact 4: 5-7 EUV layers) by making its intrinsic defectivity acceptable through matched decoding.

title: Kintsugi spares: repair rows built from a stronger cell technology
idea: Kintsugi mends pottery with gold so the repair is the strongest part; instead of spare rows from the same weak array, put repair capacity as SRAM or oxide gain-cell rows on the hybrid-bonded base die, so failed or weak rows remap to cells with no retention tail and no hammer sensitivity.
why: Frees the 2-5% of array area spent on in-array redundancy and gives repairs that never fail again, so more retention-tail rows can be retired (fact 3).

title: Tempered write: overdriven restore for rows predicted to idle
idea: Tempered glass is pre-stressed to resist cracking; when the controller predicts a row will sit idle (freshly written cold data), it issues a 'tempered' restore with boosted array voltage or longer write-recovery from a pump, storing ~20-30% more charge so the row can skip several refresh cycles.
why: Extends retention of idle data and reduces refresh count (fact 3) at the cost of rare high-energy writes; ~1.5-2x refresh reduction for cold memory.

title: Sacrificial-anode collector implants absorb hammer-injected electrons
idea: Galvanising protects steel with a zinc anode that corrodes first; add a shallow grounded n+ collector ribbon (or biased deep well) between adjacent active regions in the buried-channel array so electrons emitted by aggressor wordline traps and passing-gate charge pumping are collected before they reach a victim storage node.
why: Attacks a physical root cause of row hammer (fact 9), possibly raising the threshold 5-20x and removing counter and refresh overhead at a modest density cost.

title: Kanban charge-bucket counters: analog leaky integrators per row group
idea: Kanban cards cap work in progress; give each row group a tiny capacitor that receives a fixed charge packet on every activation and leaks with a ~32 ms time constant, and a comparator fires neighbour refresh when the bucket crosses threshold, making an analog activation counter with built-in decay and no SRAM counter tables.
why: Per-row hammer counting costs counter bits and read-modify-write timing; analog buckets cost one capacitor and comparator per group and no bandwidth (fact 9) at under 1% area.

title: Factory-seconds grade: sell retention-weak dies as inference memory
idea: Like garment 'seconds', create a product grade for dies that fail the 64 ms/85C retention spec or exceed repair, sold with a qualified controller profile (32 ms refresh, page-retirement list, on-module strong ECC) for AI inference and caches where data is rewritten constantly.
why: Turns scrap (several % of output, more on new 3D nodes) into immediate supply, raising usable bits per wafer with no capex (scarcity, cost per bit).

title: Retread memory: remanufacture retired server DRAM inside ECC shells
idea: Like tyre retreading, harvest DDR4/DDR5 from retired servers, re-test and re-bin at die or package level, and remount it on CXL expanders whose buffer chip adds strong symbol ECC, scrubbing and page retirement to absorb ageing errors.
why: Hyperscalers retire exabytes of DRAM every 4-6 years; recovering even 30% adds supply with near-zero new wafers, helium or EUV (scarcity, cost).

title: Self-clearing capacitor electrodes isolate dielectric breakdown spots
idea: Metallised film capacitors self-heal because a breakdown vaporises the ultra-thin electrode around the fault; make the DRAM pillar's inner electrode a thin oxidisable film (e.g., TiN with a thin Al skin) so a test-time 'clearing' pulse oxidises or opens the electrode locally around a leakage path, turning a dead leaky cell into a slightly smaller working one.
why: Converts dielectric-leakage tail cells into usable cells and lets thinner, higher-k, more defective dielectrics be used for more Cs (facts 1, 3); target ~10x fewer leakage-tail failures.

title: Letterpress fingerprint remap: nanoimprint template defects fixed once for all dies
idea: Worn letterpress type repeats the same blemish on every page; pattern critical array layers by nanoimprint cured with 365 nm UV-LEDs (no ArF/KrF excimers, which burn neon, argon and krypton), map the template's defects once, and burn one shared fuse remap into every die that template stamps, since its defects land at identical coordinates.
why: Removes neon-dependent litho and turns NIL's main weakness, repeating template defects, into a one-time characterisation instead of per-die yield loss; litho capex could fall by half (fact 4).

title: Supercritical-CO2 decaffeination-style healing of capacitor dielectric vacancies
idea: Coffee is decaffeinated by supercritical CO2 that penetrates whole beans; use scCO2 carrying trace H2O2 or ozone, with no argon plasma or anneal ambient, to reach the bottom of 70:1 capacitor trenches at under 150C and refill oxygen vacancies in ZrO2/HfO2 that create the leakage tail.
why: Tightens the dielectric leakage tail (facts 1, 3) with a low-temperature, rare-gas-free step compatible with BEOL and 3D tiers; target 2-5x fewer tail cells.

title: Quench-tank immersion screening profiles retention of whole wafers
idea: Like quenching a batch of parts in an oil tank, immerse whole wafers in a temperature-controlled dielectric-fluid bath (no helium backside chucks or He-cooled thermal heads) and run massively parallel retention and hammer profiling at 95C through probe cards, producing a full weak-cell map per die.
why: A cheap, uniform thermal soak lets every die ship with its retention map (enabling refresh-skipping schemes) and takes helium out of test; cuts test capital per bit.

title: Cast multicrystalline array wafers with grain-boundary-aware row retirement
idea: For the array wafer of a hybrid-bonded array/periphery split, replace argon-purged Czochralski pulling and Spruce Pine quartz crucibles with directional casting under vacuum/N2 in silicon-nitride-coated crucibles, as solar does; photoluminescence-image every wafer's grain boundaries and retire or remap the mats and rows that cross them, since boundaries mostly create leakage-tail cells.
why: Removes two chokepoints (argon, high-purity quartz) and cuts substrate cost several-fold, using reliability mapping to make imperfect silicon acceptable.

title: Anodised self-reforming capacitors like aluminium electrolytics
idea: Electrolytic capacitors heal oxide flaws by re-anodising under bias; grow the cell dielectric by wet anodisation of an electroless or N2-purged ALD Ta/Nb/Hf film (no argon sputtering or plasma), leaving a thin ion-supply layer so periodic in-field 'reforming' pulses re-oxidise new leakage spots.
why: A rare-gas-free dielectric route with a built-in self-healing loop against leakage-tail drift (fact 3); anodic Nb/Ta oxides at k~25-40 also raise Cs (fact 1).

title: Lumber-grade radial zones: extra redundancy designed into wafer-edge fields
idea: Sawmills grade heartwood and sapwood differently; when helium backside cooling is replaced by electrostatic chucks with hydrogen or conductive-elastomer contact, accept wider centre-to-edge CD drift and print two reticle designs, full-density centre fields and edge-ring fields with 2x spare rows/columns and stronger on-die ECC.
why: Makes helium-free thermal control yield-neutral by spending redundancy only where non-uniformity lives, keeping ~90-95% of the wafer at full density.

title: Watertight-bulkhead subarrays with current-limit breakers contain metal shorts
idea: Ships survive hull breaches through watertight bulkheads; since argon-free metallisation (N2-reactive or CVD/ALD-only with no Ar PVD) can raise particle and short rates, give each subarray its own power and wordline-pump domain behind a self-resetting current-limit switch, so one short is isolated and the mat is retired instead of sinking the die.
why: Turns die-killing shorts into a loss of 1/N capacity, keeping rare-gas-free metallisation yield-viable; partially good dies ship at a lower density grade.

title: Lost-foam air gaps between buried wordlines via oxygen ash
idea: Lost-foam casting burns out a foam pattern to leave a cavity; deposit a carbon or polymer spacer between buried wordlines, cap it with porous oxide, then burn it out with an O2 ash (no argon sputter or plasma), leaving vacuum gaps that cut wordline-to-wordline and passing-gate coupling.
why: Lower coupling could raise the row-hammer threshold ~3-10x (fact 9) and cut wordline capacitance and energy (fact 10), all without rare gases.

title: Micro-Czochralski seed dots grown with green solid-state lasers
idea: Copy crystal pulling at micron scale: etch seed holes in each 3D tier's oxide, deposit amorphous Si, and melt it with a 532 nm diode-pumped solid-state laser (not a XeCl excimer, which needs xenon and neon) so each grain grows from its own seed and every access transistor sits inside a single grain.
why: Grain boundaries drive the leakage tail of poly-Si tier transistors (facts 2, 3); location-controlled grains could let lateral 3D access transistors meet the <13 fA tail without rare-gas lasers.

title: Melt-pool-style monitoring: test each 3D tier before it is buried
idea: Metal 3D printers watch every layer's melt pool; after each 3D-DRAM tier is patterned, scan it with e-beam voltage-contrast inspection (no xenon plasma FIB or rare-gas plasma) to map opens and shorts, and program that tier's remap into antifuses or a base-die table before the next tier covers it.
why: Tier defects compound over 26+ tiers (fact 2); knowing them in-line lets the stack repair instead of scrap, flattening 3D yield loss.

title: Self-healing microcapsule underfill for hybrid-bonded memory stacks
idea: Self-healing concrete and composites release a healing agent when cracks open; fill HBM/3D-stack gaps with underfill holding microcapsules of low-viscosity resin plus dispersed catalyst that rupture at TSV or micro-bump cracks during thermal cycling and re-bond them, using no rare-gas processing.
why: Reduces TSV/bump field failures and cycling yield loss (fact 6: 20-30% yield hit), allowing thinner, cheaper stacks with less conservative design margins.

title: Inkjet nanoparticle repair of interposer and module opens
idea: Display makers repair TFT line opens by direct printing; after test, inkjet silver or copper nanoparticle ink to bridge open RDL/interposer lines or rewire to spare channels, cured by low-temperature chemical (halide) sintering or IR diodes, avoiding xenon flash lamps and argon-carrier laser-CVD repair.
why: Rescues stacks and modules with a single open (fact 6), adding several points of assembled-HBM yield at no rare-gas cost.

title: Ladder-stop segmented vertical bitlines tolerate argon-free metal fill voids
idea: A dropped stitch runs the whole knit column unless loops lock; because argon-free fill (CVD/ALD in N2/H2 with no PVD liner) leaves more voids in tall vertical bitlines, split each vertical bitline into 8-tier segments joined by lockable switch transistors, so a void or open loses one segment, which is remapped to a spare.
why: Lets 3D DRAM tolerate the defect density of rare-gas-free metallisation (fact 2), limiting a single open to ~1/N of the string instead of the whole column.

title: Spun-yarn bits: one bit's charge summed across several tiers
idea: Yarn spins many weak fibres into a strong thread; store each bit on 3-4 small capacitors in successive tiers sharing one vertical bitline and fired together, so a single leaky transistor from low-temperature, rare-gas-free tier deposition only shaves a fraction of the signal.
why: Averaging suppresses the leakage tail (fact 3) roughly by the fibre count and sums Cs across tiers to beat the charge wall (fact 1) without high aspect ratio; trades per-tier density for many cheap tiers.

title: Nitrogen-deuterium hot isostatic press closes voids and passivates traps
idea: Castings are HIPed under argon to close porosity; instead, HIP finished DRAM wafers in 10-20 bar D2/N2 with no argon, so deuterium passivates interface traps (D-Si bonds resist hot-carrier and hammer-driven breaking better than H-Si) and the pressure collapses voids in capacitor fill.
why: Narrower leakage tail plus better hot-carrier and hammer robustness (facts 3, 9), rare-gas-free; target ~30% less refresh.

title: Carbon-implant proximity gettering beneath bonded array tiers
idea: Gettering is the fab's filter press; implant carbon (not argon or xenon pre-amorphisation) a few microns beneath each bonded or layer-transferred array tier, creating sinks that pull Fe, Ni and Cu out of storage-node junctions during low-temperature anneals.
why: Metal contamination is a prime source of retention-tail junction leakage, worse in low-thermal-budget 3D flows (facts 2, 3); image sensors cut dark current ~10x this way.

title: Vernier-select contacts absorb misregistration from solid-state interference lithography
idea: A machinist's vernier reads alignment from offset scales; pattern the periodic array with solid-state-laser interference lithography (quadrupled Nd:YAG, no excimer neon), print periphery contacts as a vernier set of offset candidates, and after test electrically select whichever candidate landed on each line.
why: Interference litho makes cheap, rare-gas-free gratings but registers poorly to separately patterned periphery; vernier selection turns overlay error into a fuse choice, cutting litho capital (fact 4).

title: Catalyst-regeneration detrap pulses during refresh idle
idea: Refineries burn coke off catalysts to restore activity; because rare-gas-free cell and gate dielectrics (no argon plasma densification) start with more traps, apply periodic negative-bias 'regeneration' pulses on idle wordlines to empty the filled traps behind VRT and gate-induced drain leakage.
why: Holds the leakage tail near its fresh-state value over life (fact 3) so cheaper rare-gas-free dielectrics can qualify; target ~1.5x longer refresh period.

title: Shipping-container reliability shell for alt-fab memory dies
idea: Containerisation let any cargo ride any ship; define a standard CXL buffer-chip 'container' (strong symbol ECC, scrubbing, page retirement, refresh management) so dies from new rare-gas-free alt-fabs (NIL, DSA, interference litho, UV-LED lines) plug into servers interchangeably despite raw BER ~100x worse than DDR5.
why: Lets fabs with no neon or helium dependence sell bits immediately, expanding U.S.-manufacturable supply (scarcity, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Microwave kiln anneal heals implant damage in upper tiers
idea: Ceramic makers sinter in microwave kilns; activate dopants and heal implant damage in 3D tiers with 5.8 GHz microwave annealing at ~400-500C, replacing excimer melt-laser anneals (xenon/neon) and argon RTP, so end-of-range defects that cause junction leakage are repaired without cooking lower tiers.
why: Lower junction leakage tail in stacked tiers (facts 2, 3) at a rare-gas-free, low thermal budget; enables more tiers without retention loss.

title: Felted fountain-coded pages for UV-LED-printed defect-dense arrays
idea: Felt is strong because random fibres overlap; store each 4 KB page as fountain-coded fragments across 18-20 subarrays so any 16 rebuild it, letting arrays patterned by 365 nm UV-LED lithography with self-aligned spacer pitch division (no Hg-Xe lamps or excimers) carry whole dead subarrays without spare mapping.
why: Defect-dense, cheap rare-gas-free litho becomes usable for a capacity tier behind cache, tolerating ~15-20% subarray loss (capital, scarcity).

title: Sous-vide chilled DRAM using absorption chillers, not cryogens
idea: Sous vide holds food at an exact temperature; hold memory modules at a precise 5-10C with waste-heat-driven lithium-bromide/water absorption chillers (no helium cryogenics) and program refresh from measured temperature, since retention roughly doubles per 10C drop.
why: Refresh can relax ~8x versus 85C, cutting refresh power and bandwidth (fact 3) by ~85% and letting weak tail cells pass, powered by data-centre waste heat.

title: Riveted hybrid bonds: redundant pads with nitrogen plasma activation
idea: Shipbuilders put several rivets in every joint so one failure is harmless; activate hybrid-bond surfaces with N2/O2 plasma (no argon) and give each critical vertical signal three parallel bond pads feeding a majority/OR receiver, so voids from the gentler activation never open a circuit.
why: Makes argon-free bonding yield-safe for HBM and 3D stacks (fact 6: 20-30% yield loss), turning single-pad voids into non-events.
